--- PDF page 4 ---
Why is alignment hard?
Reward misspeci cation
• Dif cult to capture and balance complex preferences
• Edge cases, side effects, and reward hacking
• Challenging to infer from demonstrations

Policy learning failures
• Poor choice of state/action representation
• RL algorithm can perform arbitrarily poorly
• Distribution shift

Veri cation dif culty
• Exhaustive testing not typically possible

fi

fi

fi

fi

• Lack of ground truth data to compare against

--- PDF page 5 ---
What is an alignment guarantee?

Guarantee = Metric + Con dence + Assumptions
Metric: A measure of alignment / performance
• E.g. Return of a policy under the (unknown) ground truth reward function

Con dence: A bound (often probabilistic) on a statistic of the metric
• E.g. 95% con dence bound on the expected return

Assumptions: The assumptions under which con dence is accurate

fi

fi

fi

fi

• E.g. Reward is a linear function of known features

--- PDF page 7 ---
Central claim:
Strong guarantees aren’t always possible, but value alignment
research should aim to provide the strongest guarantees that
any given setting allows, with as few assumptions as possible.

--- PDF page 8 ---
Are alignment guarantees needed?
Practicality and deployability

Safety and social harm prevention

Existential risk

Opinion: If we can’t provide alignment guarantees, then the core motivations
for alignment research can’t be fully addressed

--- PDF page 10 ---
Ef cient value alignment veri cation: A driver’s test for AI

• What if we want to verify reward or policy alignment of a
semi-blackbox agent?
• We don’t want to require policy rollouts, due to both
safety and ef ciency concerns.
• Can we design a driver’s test — a small set of (various
types of) questions to ask an agent that verify alignment?

fi

fi
